content:
This month, Google launched the all-new Pixel 11 series. Compared with last year's Pixel 10 lineup, the phones themselves haven't changed much, but there are some welcome refinements to the experience. One of them is a new camera processing option that lets you take more granular control over the final look of your photos.

Ahead of the iPhone 18 Pro launch, here's hoping Apple does something similar.

Pixel 11 adds a new camera feature called Camera Looks. It's similar in some ways to Photographic Styles on iPhone, letting you adjust how the camera processes the image before you take the photo. Because the adjustments happen before capture, it's much more than just a filter.

Google offers several presets, similar to Apple, and takes it further by letting you fine-tune each one. Beyond that, there are some fresh styles that align with modern trends in mobile photography: Editorial, Velvet, Classic, Digi, Black Tie, and Minimal.

These styles step away from the heavily-processed look of smartphone photos and try to recreate the feel of older photographs. Digi, as the name suggests, focuses on delivering the limited dynamic range, high contrast, and noisy look of those tiny point-and-shoot cameras from the 2010s.

Minimal, on the other hand, is all about low processing across the board. Many HDR processes don't kick in, and you're getting closer to what the smartphone sensor actually captured. You can check out some sample photos over at 9to5Google.

Using ProRAW on iPhone does let you dial things back to a less-processed state, but then the whole point of using a smartphone camera is kind of lost.

Wrap up

If Apple wants to build the best camera in a pocket, it has to accept that not every user has the same needs. Photographic Styles was a good start, but Apple should go further. Photography is, at its core, a form of self-expression, so giving users more choice over how much processing happens is an important next step. Apple should take a page out of Google's book and add a Minimal style to iPhone.

What do you think of iPhone photography right now? Do you like Apple's latest Photographic Styles, or do you think they still fall short? Let us know in the comments.
